subject: maths
title: Primary 2 Picture Graphs
seo_title: P2 Picture Graphs Worksheets: Free Primary 2 Maths with Answers (MOE Syllabus)
standard_text: Reading and interpreting data from picture graphs with scales
meta_desc: Free P2 maths practice on picture graphs with scales of 1, 2, 5 and 10: reading the key, most and fewest, how many more, totals. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Read the key first, then count in its steps.
key_sub: If each picture stands for 5, a row of 4 pictures shows 5, 10, 15, 20: that is 20, not 4.
body_html:
What is a picture graph?

A picture graph uses pictures to show data. Each row is one group. The key tells you what one picture stands for. Always read the key first.

Picture graphs with a scale

A picture can stand for more than 1, like 2, 5 or 10. Then count in 2s, 5s or 10s along the row.

Key: each picture stands for4 pictures showCount
141, 2, 3, 4
282, 4, 6, 8
5205, 10, 15, 20
104010, 20, 30, 40
Read a row

In the recess food graph, how many students chose prata?

Prata has 4 pictures. Each picture stands for 5. Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20.

Answer: 20 students

Most, fewest, how many more, altogether

The longest row is the most. The shortest row is the fewest. For how many more, subtract. For altogether, add.

Altogether

How many students chose chicken rice or nasi lemak?

Chicken rice: 30. Nasi lemak: 3 pictures = 15. Add: 30 + 15 = 45.

Answer: 45 students

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting the pictures: prata has 4 pictures, so 4 studentsUse the key: 4 pictures × 5 = 20 students
Not reading the key at allRead the key first: each picture may stand for 2, 5 or 10
Giving the difference in pictures: 2 more pictures, so 2 more2 more pictures × 5 = 10 more students
Adding when the question asks “how many more”How many more means subtract
Leaving out a row in a totalAdd every row, then check you used them all

faq.q: What is taught in P2 picture graphs?
faq.a: Primary 2 students read picture graphs where one picture stands for 1, 2, 5 or 10. They find the most and the fewest, how many more and how many altogether, and solve simple word problems.

faq.q: How do I explain a picture graph with a scale to my child?
faq.a: Point to the key first and say what one picture stands for, for example 5 students. Then count along the row in 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake in picture graphs?
faq.a: Counting the pictures and forgetting the key. If each picture stands for 5 and a row has 4 pictures, the answer is 20, not 4.

faq.q: Are picture graphs in the MOE syllabus for Primary 2?
faq.a: Yes. Picture graphs with scales are in the Statistics strand of the MOE 2021 Primary 2 Mathematics syllabus. Bar graphs come later, in Primary 3.

sets.title: Most, fewest and how many more

items.q: Which food is the most popular?
items.e: The longest row has the most pictures. Chicken rice has 8 pictures, which is 40 students. All the pictures stand for the same number, so you can compare the rows.

items.q: Which food is the least popular?
items.e: The shortest row has the fewest pictures. Laksa has 4 pictures, which is 20 students. All the pictures stand for the same number, so you can compare the rows.

items.q: How many more students chose chicken rice than laksa?
items.e: Chicken rice: 40 students. Laksa: 20 students. Subtract: 40 − 20 = 20. Or: Chicken rice has 4 pictures more, and 4 × 5 = 20. Do not stop at 4.

items.q: How many more students chose satay than fish soup?
items.e: Satay: 30 students. Fish soup: 25 students. Subtract: 30 − 25 = 5. Or: Satay has 1 picture more, and 1 × 5 = 5. Do not stop at 1.

items.q: How many fewer students chose satay than chicken rice?
items.e: Chicken rice: 40 students. Satay: 30 students. Subtract: 40 − 30 = 10. Or: Chicken rice has 2 pictures more, and 2 × 5 = 10. Do not stop at 2.

items.q: On which day were the most durians sold?
items.e: The longest row has the most pictures. Saturday has 9 pictures, which is 90 durians. All the pictures stand for the same number, so you can compare the rows.

items.q: On which day were the fewest durians sold?
items.e: The shortest row has the fewest pictures. Monday has 3 pictures, which is 30 durians. All the pictures stand for the same number, so you can compare the rows.

items.q: How many more durians were sold on Saturday than on Friday?
items.e: Saturday: 90 durians. Friday: 60 durians. Subtract: 90 − 60 = 30. Or: Saturday has 3 pictures more, and 3 × 10 = 30. Do not stop at 3.

items.q: How many more durians were sold on Sunday than on Monday?
items.e: Sunday: 80 durians. Monday: 30 durians. Subtract: 80 − 30 = 50. Or: Sunday has 5 pictures more, and 5 × 10 = 50. Do not stop at 5.

items.q: How many fewer durians were sold on Monday than on Saturday?
items.e: Saturday: 90 durians. Monday: 30 durians. Subtract: 90 − 30 = 60. Or: Saturday has 6 pictures more, and 6 × 10 = 60. Do not stop at 6.

items.q: How many more students go home by school bus than by MRT?
items.e: School bus: 35 students. MRT: 20 students. Subtract: 35 − 20 = 15. Or: School bus has 3 pictures more, and 3 × 5 = 15. Do not stop at 3.

items.q: How many more students go home by car than by MRT?
items.e: Car: 30 students. MRT: 20 students. Subtract: 30 − 20 = 10. Or: Car has 2 pictures more, and 2 × 5 = 10. Do not stop at 2.

items.q: How many fewer students walk home than go home by car?
items.e: Car: 30 students. Walk: 10 students. Subtract: 30 − 10 = 20. Or: Car has 4 pictures more, and 4 × 5 = 20. Do not stop at 4.

items.q: Which way home has 15 more students than MRT?
items.e: MRT has 20 students. 20 + 15 = 35. School bus has 7 pictures. Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. So the answer is school bus. (Car has 30, which is only 10 more.)

items.q: Jun Jie says, “Car has 2 more pictures than MRT, so 2 more students go home by car.” How many more students really go home by car than by MRT?
items.e: Each picture stands for 5 students, so 2 more pictures is 5 + 5 = 10 students. Car: 30. MRT: 20. 30 − 20 = 10. Jun Jie counted pictures and forgot the key.

items.q: How many students chose red or blue?
items.e: Red: 12. Blue: 16. Add: 12 + 16 = 28. Or count all 14 pictures in 2s.

items.q: How many students chose yellow or green?
items.e: Yellow: 6. Green: 10. Add: 6 + 10 = 16. Or count all 8 pictures in 2s.

items.q: How many students chose a colour altogether?
items.e: Add all the rows: 12 + 16 + 6 + 10 = 44. Or: there are 22 pictures, and each stands for 2. 22 pictures is not 22.

items.q: How many students did not choose blue?
items.e: Add the other rows: 12 + 6 + 10 = 28. Or take away from the total: 44 − 16 = 28.

items.q: Which two colours were chosen by 26 students altogether?
items.e: Blue: 16. Green: 10. 16 + 10 = 26. Red and blue make 28, and red and green make 22, and so do blue and yellow.

items.q: How many shells did Chloe and Ahmad find altogether?
items.e: Chloe: 35. Ahmad: 20. Add: 35 + 20 = 55. Or count all 11 pictures in 5s.

items.q: How many shells did Mei Ling and Kumar find altogether?
items.e: Mei Ling: 30. Kumar: 15. Add: 30 + 15 = 45. Or count all 9 pictures in 5s.

items.q: How many shells did they find altogether?
items.e: Add all the rows: 35 + 20 + 30 + 15 = 100. Or: there are 20 pictures, and each stands for 5. 20 pictures is not 20.

items.q: Who found more shells: Chloe, or Ahmad and Kumar together?
items.e: Chloe found 35 shells. Ahmad and Kumar found 20 + 15 = 35 shells. 35 = 35, so they found the same. Ahmad and Kumar have 7 pictures together, the same as Chloe.

items.q: How many shells did the other three children find, not counting Mei Ling?
items.e: Add the other rows: 35 + 20 + 15 = 70. Or take away from the total: 100 − 30 = 70.

items.q: How many visitors came on Monday and Tuesday altogether?
items.e: Monday: 40. Tuesday: 60. Add: 40 + 60 = 100. Or count all 10 pictures in 10s.

items.q: How many visitors came on Wednesday and Thursday altogether?
items.e: Wednesday: 80. Thursday: 50. Add: 80 + 50 = 130. Or count all 13 pictures in 10s.

items.q: How many visitors came in the four days altogether?
items.e: Add all the rows: 40 + 60 + 80 + 50 = 230. Or: there are 23 pictures, and each stands for 10. 23 pictures is not 23.

items.q: How many visitors came on the days other than Wednesday?
items.e: Add the other rows: 40 + 60 + 50 = 150. Or take away from the total: 230 − 80 = 150.

items.q: How many visitors came from Monday to Wednesday?
items.e: Monday to Wednesday is 3 days: 40 + 60 + 80 = 180. Do not add Thursday. (18 is the number of pictures.)

items.q: The P2 students chose their favourite recess food. How many more students chose chicken rice than nasi lemak?
items.e: Chicken rice: 8 pictures = 40. Nasi lemak: 3 pictures = 15. 40 − 15 = 25. (5 is the difference in pictures, and 55 is what you get if you add.)

items.q: How many students did not choose chicken rice?
items.e: Add the other rows: 25 + 35 + 15 = 75. Or: 115 − 40 = 75. (15 is the number of pictures in the other rows.)

items.q: On Friday, 10 more students chose prata. How many pictures should prata have now?
items.e: Prata had 35. 35 + 10 = 45 students. Each picture stands for 5: 45 is 9 fives. So prata needs 9 pictures, 2 more than before. (7 + 10 = 17 forgets the key.)

items.q: Which two foods were chosen by 60 students altogether?
items.e: Fried noodles 25 + prata 35 = 60. Chicken rice and prata make 75, prata and nasi lemak make 50, and fried noodles and nasi lemak make 40.

items.q: Ryan says, “7 students chose prata.” What mistake did he make?
c: He did not use the key
items.e: Ryan counted 7 pictures. But each picture stands for 5 students: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35. So 35 students chose prata. He did not use the key.

items.q: The canteen cooks 30 plates of fried noodles. Each student who chose fried noodles gets 1 plate. How many plates are left?
items.e: Fried noodles has 5 pictures, so 25 students chose it. 30 − 25 = 5 plates left. (30 − 5 = 25 uses the pictures, not the students.)

items.q: How many students were asked altogether?
items.e: Add all the rows: 40 + 25 + 35 + 15 = 115. (23 is the number of pictures, and 100 leaves out nasi lemak.)

items.q: Four friends read books in the June holidays. Who read 4 more books than Raju?
items.e: Raju read 8 books. 8 + 4 = 12. Ali has 6 pictures: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. So Ali read 12. 4 more books is only 2 more pictures.

items.q: Raju wants to read as many books as Mei Ling. How many more books must he read?
items.e: Mei Ling read 18. Raju read 8. 18 − 8 = 10 books. (5 is the difference in pictures.)

items.q: How many books did Ali and Chloe read altogether?
items.e: Ali: 12. Chloe: 14. 12 + 14 = 26 books. (13 is the number of pictures.)

items.q: In July, Mei Ling read 6 fewer books than in June. How many pictures are needed for her July row?
items.e: June: 18 books. 18 − 6 = 12 books in July. Each picture stands for 2, so 12 needs 6 pictures. (9 − 6 = 3 takes 6 pictures away instead of 6 books.)

items.q: How many fewer books did Raju read than Chloe?
items.e: Chloe: 14. Raju: 8. 14 − 8 = 6 books. Raju has 3 fewer pictures, and 3 × 2 = 6.

items.q: The four friends want to read 60 books altogether. How many more books must they read?
items.e: Total so far: 12 + 18 + 8 + 14 = 52. 60 − 52 = 8 books. (60 − 26 pictures = 34 forgets the key.)

items.q: Hafiz read 16 books in June. How many pictures should be drawn for him?
items.e: Each picture stands for 2 books. Count in 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. That is 8 pictures. (32 is 16 × 2: do not multiply.)

items.q: In a picture graph, each picture stands for 5 stickers. Siti has 6 pictures. Ahmad has 10 more stickers than Siti. How many stickers does Ahmad have?
items.e: Siti: 6 pictures × 5 = 30 stickers. Ahmad has 10 more: 30 + 10 = 40 stickers. (6 + 10 = 16 forgets the key.)

items.q: Each picture stands for 10 marbles. Kumar has 4 pictures and Devi has 7 pictures. How many marbles do they have altogether?
items.e: Kumar: 4 tens = 40. Devi: 7 tens = 70. 40 + 70 = 110 marbles. Or: 11 pictures × 10 = 110. (11 counts pictures; 30 subtracts.)

items.q: Xin Yi made a picture graph. Each picture stands for 2 students. Prata has 8 pictures and laksa has 5 pictures. How many more students chose prata than laksa?
items.e: Prata: 8 × 2 = 16. Laksa: 5 × 2 = 10. The model shows 16 − 10 = 6 students. (3 is the difference in pictures.)

items.q: Mr Tan’s class has 40 students. In a picture graph, each picture stands for 2 students. There are 15 pictures for “Walk”. The rest take the bus. How many students take the bus?
items.e: Walk: 15 × 2 = 30 students. Bus: 40 − 30 = 10 students. (40 − 15 = 25 uses the pictures, not the students.)

items.q: The canteen sold 45 cups of Milo. In a picture graph, each picture stands for 5 cups. How many pictures are drawn for Milo?
items.e: Count in 5s until you reach 45: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45. That is 9 pictures.

items.q: Priya drew a picture graph of 30 students. Each picture stands for 10 students. How many pictures did she draw?
items.e: Count in 10s: 10, 20, 30. That is 3 pictures. 30 pictures would show 300 students.
